st-1.title: Scope rules for every agent carrying this document
st-1.note: The prompt is loaded as system context by the orchestrator and by every sub-agent at every depth, so it opens by disambiguating who owes what. Standards (verification, measurement, safety, reporting) bind universally; side effects (Slack, Drive, spending, cancelling siblings) belong only to whoever's task brief grants them. Without this block a 50-agent swarm would post 50 kickoff messages.

st-3.title: The task, in one sentence
st-3.note: Template slot TASK_TARGET. Fixes the modality (de novo miniprotein binders), the method family (structure-based design-and-filter), and two competing objectives: peak affinity zero-shot AND high hit rate. Optimising only for the top design would satisfy goal 1 and fail goal 2, which is why the deliverable is 30 ranked designs rather than one.

st-5.title: Target dossier and the human comparison arm
st-5.note: Template slot TARGET_DOSSIER: accession, oligomeric state, and constitutive cofactor, which downstream sections convert into hard scoring-construct requirements. The competition link establishes that human expert teams are working the same target, framing this as a benchmarked comparison rather than an open-ended exercise.

st-7.title: Reference access policy and the offline corpus
st-7.note: Every cited source is mirrored in the bundled corpus, so a paywall or dead link does not excuse skipping a reference. Names the entry point (_MASTER_SOURCE_INDEX) and notes that large PDFs are page-split. This addresses a common failure mode where an agent omits an input it could not retrieve.

st-9.title: Ref 1: BenchBB benchmark
st-9.note: Adaptyv's community benchmark for binder design; establishes what hit rates are achievable and how the assay that will score these designs actually works.

st-10.title: Ref 2: Protein Optimization 101
st-10.note: First of a four-part Adaptyv primer series. Practitioner-level guidance on binder optimisation, included so the agent inherits community craft knowledge rather than reasoning from papers alone.

st-11.title: Ref 3: Protein Optimization 102
st-11.note: Continuation of the optimisation primer. Relevant to the mandatory in silico optimization rounds specified later.

st-12.title: Ref 4: Protein Optimization 103
st-12.note: Third part of the primer series.

st-13.title: Ref 5: Has binder design been solved?
st-13.note: Adaptyv's assessment of the field's current ceiling. Frames how much headroom a campaign like this can expect, and what counts as a good result.

st-14.title: Ref 6: MBP case study with BindCraft
st-14.note: A worked end-to-end case study on one target. The closest thing in the reference set to a template for the campaign's own workflow.

st-15.title: Ref 7: Crowdsourced design, EGFR competition preprint
st-15.note: The peer-reviewable write-up of a large crowdsourced binder competition. Supplies measured in vitro outcomes for a wide range of methods against one target.

st-16.title: Ref 8: EGFR competition round 1 data
st-16.note: ProteinBase collection with per-design sequences and measured binding. Doubles as known-binder corpus material for the novelty gate.

st-17.title: Ref 9: EGFR competition round 2 data
st-17.note: Second round of the same competition; shows how much the field improved between rounds.

st-18.title: Ref 10: Agents vs Humans
st-18.note: Directly relevant prior art: an evaluation of whether LLM agents can design proteins competitively with humans. This campaign is a scaled-up instance of that question.

st-19.title: Ref 11: MUNI hackathon submissions
st-19.note: The underlying per-design data for the agents-vs-humans comparison.

st-20.title: Ref 12: TREM2 competition
st-20.note: One of the campaign's own 14 targets, previously run as a public competition. Provides both a difficulty prior and known binders to exclude on novelty grounds.

st-21.title: Ref 13: Myostatin / GDF-8 competition
st-21.note: Prior art for the GDF-8 target, which is the only target in the set carrying a selectivity requirement against a close paralog.

st-22.title: Ref 14: GEM x Adaptyv RBX1 competition
st-22.note: Competition announcement for RBX1, a zinc-coordinating RING domain: the target that most stresses the cofactor-representation rules below.

st-24.title: Ref 16: RBX1 all submissions
st-24.note: Full submission set including failures, which is the more informative half for calibrating expected hit rate.

st-25.title: Ref 17: Nipah-G submissions overview
st-25.note: Editorial overview of the Nipah-G competition submissions.

st-26.title: Ref 18: Nipah-G competition
st-26.note: Competition page for the Nipah-G attachment glycoprotein target.

st-27.title: Ref 19: Nipah-G results
st-27.note: Measured binding outcomes for Nipah-G designs.

st-28.title: Ref 20: Nipah-G all submissions
st-28.note: Complete Nipah-G submission set, hits and misses.

st-29.title: Ref 21: RFdiffusion re-validation
st-29.note: An independent wet-lab re-run of RFdiffusion designs. It separates published performance from reproducible performance, the exact distinction required in the Verification section.

st-30.title: Ref 22: BindCraft v1 re-validation
st-30.note: The same independent re-validation treatment applied to BindCraft.

st-31.title: Ref 23: AlphaProteo technical report
st-31.note: DeepMind's binder generator. Cited for its results and filtering strategy; the model itself is not on the roster.

st-32.title: Ref 24: AlphaProteo blog
st-32.note: Accessible companion to the AlphaProteo report.

st-33.title: Ref 25: Cao et al. 2022, design from target structure alone
st-33.note: The foundational demonstration that binders can be designed from an unliganded target structure alone, which provides the premise for the campaign.

st-34.title: Ref 26: Watson et al. 2023, RFdiffusion
st-34.note: Method paper for a roster tool that is asterisked, i.e. subject to the 50-backbone-per-target floor.

st-35.title: Ref 27: Pacesa et al. 2025, BindCraft
st-35.note: Method paper for BindCraft, whose free derivative FreeBindCraft is an asterisked roster tool.

st-36.title: Ref 28: BoltzGen preprint
st-36.note: Method paper for another asterisked roster generator.

st-37.title: Ref 29: BoltzGen release designs
st-37.note: The designs provided with the BoltzGen release, usable both as a performance reference and as novelty-gate material.

st-39.title: Target dossier: the biology gate before any compute
st-39.note: Converts a literature review into machine-checked state: oligomeric state, cofactors, exact assay construct, and representative PDB depositions. The scoring construct is frozen per arm at gate time and re-asserted on every production row by parsing the output structure: chain count and cofactor atoms must match /state/gates/{target}.json or the score is written as NaN with CONSTRUCT_FAIL, never a number.

st-41.title: Design against multiple depositions, not one
st-41.note: Guards against overfitting a single crystal form. Priority goes to the structure matching the assay construct, with cross-checks against the others where affordable. Explicitly separates apo/holo conformational questions (handled by the dossier) from oligomer-modelling questions (handled at scoring).

st-43.title: Epitope selection policy
st-43.note: Prefers epitopes with design precedent and a plausible mechanism of action over novel ones, but permits novelty given a stated hypothesis. Cross-species reactivity is explicitly a secondary objective that may never compromise primary affinity or hit rate, preventing optimization for unrequested metrics.

st-45.title: Licence boundary on tooling
st-45.note: Any open-source tool with a commercially available licence is in scope; anything else is out. This one sentence is what later excludes AlphaFold3 weights, Rosetta/PyRosetta and ESM3 despite all three being obvious choices technically.

st-47.title: Roster definition as examples
st-47.note: Specifies tools in no particular order as examples rather than an exhaustive allowlist; additions are governed by the tool integration rule at line 61.

st-49.title: Structure design / co-design roster
st-49.note: Thirteen generators. The asterisk marks the seven methods subject to the 50-backbone-per-target floor enforced by the DISPATCH agent. HalluDesign and Protein Hunter are noted as wrappers hallucinating through a co-folding backbone, inheriting that backbone's dependencies.

st-50.title: FoldCraft install notes and why it is on the roster
st-50.note: Names the exact repository, records that it does not need PyRosetta (which would put it out of licence scope), and pre-empts two known install failures. The strategic reason for its inclusion: it can produce beta-containing and mixed alpha/beta folds, which is how the 10% non-all-alpha diversity target at line 69 gets met.

st-51.title: Sequence design roster
st-51.note: Names two tools, both soluble-optimized variants. Base variants are permitted for backbone search but not for designs selected for ordering, preventing CRO-level solubility failures.

st-52.title: The three-arm scoring instrument, and its substitutes
st-52.note: Splits co-folders into three tiers: the frozen three-arm ranking instrument (bring up first), substitute-only supplements usable when an arm fails on a target, and AF_Unmasked as diagnostic only. The tiering is what makes 'the instrument' a stable object that can be frozen and disclosed rather than drifting per design.

st-53.title: ESMFold2 install and inference recipe
st-53.note: Pins weights, warns that the PyPI 'esm' package is a different project, and freezes inference parameters so scores are comparable across the campaign. Declares both variants instrument backbones: failure to run them is a halt-and-post condition, not a degrade-and-continue. Also fences the pre-AF3 folder set to AlphaFold2/Multimer and reproductions.

st-54.title: Protenix v2 recipe, and the hardest bring-up gate in the prompt
st-54.note: Exact pip pin, CUDA base, checkpoint source, CLI invocation and the flags NOT to pass. Then the operational trap: the first call JIT-compiles a CUDA kernel for 4-6 minutes, so TORCH_EXTENSIONS_DIR must live on a shared persistent volume and the first canary needs a 15-minute timeout. Production generation and scoring on every target is held until this reaches roster PASS; five failed fresh-H100 attempts is a halt.

st-55.title: AlphaFold3 engine with OpenFold3 weights
st-55.note: The licence workaround: AF3's JAX code paired with open OF3 weights is fully Apache-2.0, where AF3's own weights are not. Positioned as a permissive cross-check, explicitly not allowed to displace the frozen instrument.

st-57.title: TOOL-BRINGUP stage and the sandbox-termination contract
st-57.note: Budgets the first hour to one sub-agent per roster tool plus ipSAE, MMseqs2 and DockQ, each proving a canary and leaving a run_<tool>.py on the shared volume. Direct Sandbox.create invocations must wrap termination in try/finally, while host.compute jobs are terminated by monitors upon harvest. A non-zero exit with declared output present is classified as a harvest rather than a re-run.

st-59.title: Structure-to-sequence adapters must be validated too
st-59.note: Warns against generator hazards: CA-only PDBs, non-standard residue comp_ids, and swapped chain order, all of which break sequence design without explicit errors. Adapters must be validated on a campaign target rather than testing components in isolation, preventing interface errors from surviving to production.

st-61.title: Adding tools, and the three named exclusions
st-61.note: New tools may join once a production agent has run them end to end on a real target; unverified or license-unconfirmed tools require a logged deviation rather than delivering dependent designs. AlphaFold3 weights, Rosetta/PyRosetta, and ESM3 are explicitly excluded on licensing grounds.

st-63.title: Deliverable design definition
st-63.note: Defines deliverables as single-chain miniproteins of 50-120 residues (35-160 permitted with recorded rationale). All candidates must be generated de novo; using known miniproteins, peptides, nanobodies, or antibodies as starting points or grafts is prohibited.

st-65.title: Method floor: 50 backbones per asterisked method per target
st-65.note: Anti-monoculture mechanism: DISPATCH recomputes the (target, method) count matrix every 15-minute cycle, writes it to /state/floor_matrix.json, and prioritizes under-represented cells. Throughput, GPU expense, and skill availability are rejected as grounds to skip an asterisked method. Exactly one submit-token issuer is authorized, and the orchestrator never calls submit_gate itself.

st-67.title: Target-fold mimicry failure mode
st-67.note: A generator conditioned on an oligomeric complex may reproduce a target protomer when asked for a binder of similar length, because protomers bind neighboring chains in training data. This design hazard is filtered mechanically by the TM-score branch of the novelty gate at line 81.

st-69.title: Fold diversity target: 10% non-all-alpha
st-69.note: Defined operationally via DSSP (one beta strand of 3+ consecutive E/B residues, or helical fraction below 70%) to enable automated computation. If the pool cannot achieve this without displacing superior designs, the prompt directs delivering fewer candidates with the count and reason stated.

st-71.title: Sequence design protocol
st-71.note: Soluble variants for anything headed for order; base variants fine for search. Caliby must run both fixed-backbone and over a 32-structure Protpardelle-1c ensemble per its own paper. Co-design models get scored on both their native sequence and a redesign, and cross-pipeline mixing is encouraged for diversity.

st-73.title: LCP sequence-design restraint
st-73.note: Local Composition Perplexity penalizes homopolymer stretches per position. The method is defined in Figure 1 of the kickoff materials, and lcp_score must be recorded for every designed sequence.

st-75.title: Figure 1 caption: LCP definition
st-75.note: Attached to the kickoff message rather than embedded in the markdown. The agent must read the figure to implement the penalty; there is no prose fallback.

st-77.title: Figure 2 caption: LCP results
st-77.note: Evidence that the LCP restraint improves sequence design, supplied so the requirement reads as motivated rather than arbitrary.

st-79.title: Pre-scoring filters run before any co-folding spend
st-79.note: Ordering rule with resource justification: cheap sequence filters run before expensive GPU scoring. UniRef90 staging is decoupled from initial dispatch, but full novelty verification and Ubiquitin rejection must complete before any candidate reaches the final sheet.

st-81.title: Filter 1: Novelty, with three independent thresholds
st-81.note: Checks against UniRef90, the known-binder corpus, and every chain of the target's own reference and control structures. Three rejection criteria apply: >60% identity over >50% coverage, >=30% gapped local identity over >=40 residues, or TM-score >=0.5 to any target or control chain (which intercepts target-mimic protomers). Ubiquitin receives special handling because it emerges with terminal extensions that defeat exact matching.

st-82.title: Filter 2: Developability liabilities
st-82.note: Cysteine parity, homopolymer runs, surface hydrophobic patches. Cheap sequence-level checks for the things that make a protein fail at the CRO rather than in silico.

st-83.title: Filter 3: Monomer foldability
st-83.note: Does the binder fold on its own? Threshold frozen per target at the validation gate, defaulting to mean pLDDT 70. The parenthetical about scale is a real trap: ESMFold2 emits 0-1 where most tools emit 0-100, so a naive threshold comparison would pass everything or nothing.

st-84.title: Filter 4: Structural plausibility
st-84.note: Backbone geometry, clashes, core packing. Thresholds are the agent's to choose but must be written down before production scoring begins: freezing a threshold is an explicit defense against moving the goalposts.

st-86.title: Downstream exclusion of rejected designs
st-86.note: A filtering stage is defined as complete only when rejected sequences are demonstrably absent from every downstream pool. This rule prevents filtering from being a passive logging step: the check must actively prevent bad rows from progressing.

st-88.title: Redundancy clustering, with different rules per pool type
st-88.note: De novo pools cluster at ~90% identity before scoring so near-duplicates do not consume GPU budget. Mutagenesis and close-variant pools skip that step to preserve related sequences, dropping only exact duplicates and deferring diversity enforcement to selection time.

st-90.title: Provenance keys and the frozen method vocabulary
st-90.note: root_backbone_id and structure_method are stamped at generation time and survive every downstream step, which is how diversity caps are counted. Method names are frozen tokens from method_vocab.json (rfdiffusion and rfdiffusion3 stay distinct). The sheet writer recomputes all metrics from sequence and structure, rejecting carried values that diverge by more than 1e-4.

st-92.title: Selection caps, applied in order
st-92.note: Six ceilings applied in selection order: exact duplicates, Levenshtein min-distance 5, max 5% per root backbone, max 10% per TM90 cluster, max 50% per structure method (minimum three methods), and max two-thirds per sequence method. If the ranked pool cannot fill 30 rows under these, the fix is upstream: generate more designs and test more methods, rather than relaxing caps. The relaxation ladder in st-185 is the last resort.

st-94.title: Three-arm scoring instrument, and the cofactor rule
st-94.note: The scoring ensemble is grounded in benchmark evidence showing the three tools match or exceed AlphaFold3 for de novo binder filtering across distinct seeds. Because all three tools support non-protein entities, target cofactors from the dossier must be supplied to every arm without exception.

st-96.title: The instrument, stated plainly
st-96.note: Three arms, one sample per seed: ESMFold2-Fast single-sequence, ESMFold2-Full with target MSA, Protenix v2 with target MSA. The short block that everything else in the scoring section refers back to.

st-98.title: Two-metric ranking: ipSAE and pose agreement, and the two summary scores
st-98.note: The scoring core: each arm contributes ipSAE_min and sc_DockQ against the designed complex, using that arm's own argmax-ipSAE seed and best symmetric chain relabelling, with pose_dockq defined as the minimum across arms. Two summaries are kept separate: final_score (raw mean of six terms) is the headline, while rank_zscore (4:1 ipSAE:DockQ weighted z-average) is used for ranking only. Both scoring formulas must be frozen and disclosed before production scoring.

st-100.title: Seed-tier structure
st-100.note: Header introducing the two-tier compute strategy: cheap wide screening, expensive narrow confirmation.

st-102.title: SCREEN tier: 1 seed per arm
st-102.note: The wide filter. Ranks on rank_zscore and keeps whatever top fraction the budget supports. Fast iteration is the explicit purpose; nothing at this tier is shippable.

st-103.title: INTERMEDIATE and FINAL tiers: 5 distinct seeds per arm
st-103.note: Header for the confirmation tier. 'Distinct' is enforced later by an assertion that the seed set has five unique integers and that per-design variance is non-zero.

st-104.title: Intermediate use is unrestricted
st-104.note: Five-seed scoring may be used freely between waves and optimization rounds. The only thing that distinguishes intermediate from final is which pool it ranks.

st-105.title: FINAL tier, and the frozen-mask rule
st-105.note: Defines the ranking formula: three seed-maximized ipSAE_min terms (weight 4) and three sc_DockQ terms (weight 1). When evaluating under a disclosed REDUCED_MASK, the mean includes only realized terms and score_instrument identifies them. Removing a validated arm from a frozen mask constitutes data corruption.

st-107.title: Mask freezing, and pre-registering alternative formulas
st-107.note: The per-target scoring mask freezes during validation-gate execution and is enforced programmatically by the sheet writer. Alternative ranking formulas are permitted only when demonstrably superior at separating controls, provided they are frozen and documented before production scoring.

st-109.title: Eleven co-folding considerations
st-109.note: Header for the most technically dense list in the prompt.

st-111.title: Consideration 1: The validation gate file
st-111.note: Production scoring is blocked until /state/gates/{target}.json exists with status PASS, and submit_gate() reads that file on every scoring dispatch. Two conditions must be satisfied: fold recapitulation against a named CA-RMSD threshold, and positive-control separation. If controls exist but separation fails on every instrument, self-authorization is barred and a three-step remediation ladder applies.

st-112.title: Consideration 2: Control selection, and demoting antibodies
st-112.note: Non-antibody controls are preferred because co-folding models systematically underperform on antibody-antigen interfaces, so an antibody control that fails separation is weak evidence rather than a red flag. Published de novo miniprotein binders are excluded outright as separation controls: they were themselves selected by co-folding metrics, so their separation would be circular. A rare piece of explicit reasoning about evaluation bias.

st-113.title: Consideration 3: MSA caching, and the per-arm MSA policy
st-113.note: Target-chain MSAs are staged once per target during bring-up into a shared cache that every MSA-consuming arm reads from, while binder chains are always single-sequence. Positive controls additionally receive an MSA on the control-ligand chain. Single-sequence mode for an MSA-capable arm is a per-target deviation requiring evidence and disclosure.

st-114.title: Consideration 4: Rank on ipSAE_min, shadow ipTM
st-114.note: ipTM and LIS come free from the same forward pass and are recorded, but never rank. The reason is stated: on multimeric targets whole-complex ipTM is inflated by the native protomer-protomer interfaces, compressing design-vs-control separation. If ipTM is tracked there, it must be a binder-masked variant.

st-115.title: Consideration 5: Transductive properties of z-scores
st-115.note: Because mean and standard deviation depend on the pool being scored, a z-score is comparable only within its own batch: never across targets, waves, or campaigns. Raw ipSAE_min vectors and seed counts are recorded on every row so the normalization remains reproducible.

st-116.title: Consideration 6: Pose self-consistency
st-116.note: The predicted complex must recapitulate the designed epitope rather than only scoring well. The mechanical form of this requirement is minimal and checkable: pose_dockq must be non-null on every ranked row.

st-117.title: Consideration 7: Oligomeric targets score at both 1:N and N:N
st-117.note: Template slot OLIGOMER_CLAUSE. Candidates are scored in both 1:N (which feeds rank_zscore) and N:N configurations (which records binder-binder clashes and score drops). The N:N reference complex is constructed by applying target symmetry operators to the designed pose, with symmetric relabelling.

st-118.title: Consideration 8: Non-protein context, restated
st-118.note: Reiterates mandatory inclusion of target cofactors across all scoring arms, explicitly forbidding waivers for protein-only modeling. It also notes that raw co-folding scores cannot be compared across targets, necessitating per-target z-scoring.

st-119.title: Consideration 9: No templates in production
st-119.note: Template injection is off by default. AF_Unmasked with a target template is available only as a validation-gate diagnostic when nothing else recapitulates the apo target, and is fenced out of the production scoring and pose-check path entirely.

st-120.title: Consideration 10: Check the model before blaming the model
st-120.note: Before recording that a co-folder cannot represent RNA, DNA, a ligand or an oversized chain, read the model's own paper and API rather than the campaign's wrapper around it. A missing wrapper input class is a bring-up bug; an oversized target is handled by a reasonable crop with the model kept in the panel.

st-121.title: Consideration 11: ipSAE_min defined exactly for multimers
st-121.note: Follows Dunbrack (2025): evaluation over both alignment directions, using a union-mask encompassing all target protomers with re-derived n0 and d0 parameters. Controls must use the identical construct and pairing configuration, noting that raw ipSAE values scale with chain count.

st-123.title: Calibration bands: a ceiling from nature, a floor from nonsense
st-123.note: Calibration runs provide absolute reference bounds that z-scores do not provide: an upper ceiling from native complexes (such as Barnase/Barstar) and a floor from constructed negative pairs. Controls must match production seed counts, construct definitions, and ipSAE pairing.

st-125.title: Sequence feasibility metric
st-125.note: An ESMC log-likelihood or pseudo-perplexity on every ranked design. A cheap orthogonal signal: does this sequence look like a protein to a language model, independent of whether a structure model likes its pose.

st-127.title: In silico optimization rounds
st-127.note: Feed the top outputs from one round (the best-scoring predicted complex, not the original designed structure) back into sequence design, rescore, and repeat while confidence improves, keeping every round under the same root_backbone_id so the diversity caps still bind. Minimum five rounds, continuing while metrics improve. Selection for order draws from all rounds including the original.

st-129.title: Round discipline: no optimising before you have a pool
st-129.note: Round 1 cannot start until a full generation and sequence-design wave is indexed and 1-seed screened, preventing optimization on unverified noise. Promotion to 5-seed happens before parent selection. Rows below 5 seeds are ranked below all 5-seed rows with the count disclosed rather than dropped, favoring disclosure over data deletion.

st-131.title: Nothing computed is discarded
st-131.note: Five enumerated retention classes: exact configuration including weights checksum and image digest, every structure file from every stage and seed, every metric at the level computed, the run manifest linking design to parent to job, and all logs and failure records. The stated rule (if it was computed, it is saved) makes the campaign auditable in retrospect by an external reviewer.

st-133.title: 30 designs, ordered by someone else
st-133.note: Names the two CROs and the count, then draws a hard line: the agent does not place the order. The wet-lab step stays under human control, which is also what keeps the safety framing at line 264 coherent.

st-135.title: Modal pricing and the governor arithmetic
st-135.note: Publishes the full per-second rate card and instructs verifying it at kickoff. Then derives the campaign's economics: a 4-core/32-GiB H100 box burns about $4.39/h all-in, $10,000 over 24 h is $417/h, so even pace is roughly 95 H100-equivalents and the 150-instance bootstrap cap already runs 1.58x that. max_instances is defined as a formula over the live-fleet-weighted per-sandbox rate, to be re-derived whenever the GPU mix changes.

st-137.title: The governor: the longest single block in the prompt
st-137.note: The complete spend-control system: bootstrap ramp of 25 instances per cycle to a 150 ceiling on rate-card readings tagged UNCALIBRATED, a four-condition definition of when a metered reading counts as CALIBRATED, and billing-dark alerts. Exactly four authorized writers of governor.json exist, and enforcement occurs at the submitter via submit_gate(), which is wrapped in try/except and fails closed on any exception. Logic includes a dead-man switch on stale state, live-sandbox counts with jittered backoff, and a headroom margin to absorb submission races.

st-139.title: One GPU tier: H100 only
st-139.note: A simplification argued on two grounds. H100 throughput-per-dollar is competitive with cheaper tiers once weight-load and JIT amortise, and a single tier removes both per-method tier selection and the mixed-fleet weighted-rate calculation the governor would otherwise need. A100 is a last resort.

st-141.title: Token accounting and the database query rule
st-141.note: Fresh input tokens are calculated as input_tokens minus cache_read_tokens, billing cached tokens at the cache-read rate without duplicate counting. Reported expenditure values must be calculated via server-side database SUM queries executed during message generation.

st-143.title: Scale target: 20,000 to 200,000 designs
st-143.note: A one-order-of-magnitude range rather than a number, sized to the budget. Also settles a scope question in advance: optimisation around hits counts as design work inside the campaign, not as something separate that has to be justified.

st-145.title: Design-count ledger, and why it is a tree of files
st-145.note: One JSONL file per writing frame, never a shared file, because Modal volume appends across concurrent sandboxes are not atomic and corrupt data. The coupled gen_screen job defines the unit of generation: generate, filter in-job, write survivors and the n_generated row so the method-floor matrix updates immediately, then 1-seed screen across all three arms. Chained screens dispatch immediately, and a queued-but-undrained arm is logged as a deviation.

st-147.title: Ledger semantics, and the generation backlog cap
st-147.note: Fixes the definitions of generated, screened and ranked at kickoff so campaign totals are a single aggregation rather than a matter of interpretation; any redefinition is a deviation with a reconciliation row. Several hard-won operational rules follow: never mv a shared directory while jobs write into it, route appends through the owning singleton after a fresh remount, and treat an empty ledger after a completed scoring wave as fail-loud rather than a zero. Ends with submit_gate step (d2): generation is refused once a target has 200+ generated and more than twice its scored count.

st-149.title: Resources header
st-149.note: Introduces the two-line resource list that the entire budget apparatus exists to manage.

st-151.title: $10,000 of Modal spend
st-151.note: The scalar that everything in the Compute section is derived from, and the one that changes most consequentially in the multi-target variant.

st-152.title: Practically unlimited Claude tokens
st-152.note: The resource asymmetry shaping the architecture: GPU dollars are scarce and metered, while agent tokens are not. This enables the prompt to mandate dedicated singleton sub-agents for clock, budget, watchdog, and reporting without resource restrictions.

st-154.title: BUDGET is a standing agent, not a periodic task
st-154.note: Runs the full campaign window on a 15-minute cycle and holds sole ownership of metered reads and governor writes. States the canonical-source rule plainly: the provider's metered per-job expenditure is authoritative, and rate-card figures serve only as operational cross-checks.

st-156.title: Spend to target: $10,000 is not a ceiling
st-156.note: The campaign's pacing imperative: $10,000 is a budget to spend, not a limit to stay safely below, and ending with substantial unspent funds is classified as a planning failure. The target band is +/-10% ($9k-$11k). The prompt supplies four explicit mechanisms to add work if spend lags pace: more designs, more seeds, more optimization rounds, or deeper exploration of borderline candidates.

st-158.title: Scale-up trigger: how to catch up if behind pace
st-158.note: Defines the mechanical response to falling behind: if three consecutive cycles show spend running more than 20pp below pace, or a fleet running below floor pace, scale_up_triggered() trips. The orchestrator wakes via WAKE and reallocates toward more designs, more seeds, and deeper rounds, using an evidence-weighted target_weights mechanism that balances literature difficulty priors against live campaign hit rates.

st-160.title: Generation must stay paced with scoring
st-160.note: A generated design that goes unscored is wasted compute, so the two must run at matched rates. Both directions of imbalance are reportable defects: idle GPUs while designs await scoring, and unused concurrency while jobs queue.

st-162.title: Token expenditure policy
st-162.note: The prompt emphasizes token abundance immediately before the Deliverables section, clarifying that extensive reporting and verification steps are expected rather than constrained by token limits.

st-164.title: Deliverables header
st-164.note: Splits the output into continuous deliverables (Slack, Drive) and final artefacts, both of which follow.

st-166.title: Slack updates
st-166.note: Header for the four-part communication protocol.

st-167.title: Kickoff post: the only top-level message of the campaign
st-167.note: Fixed header format including target, model, date and frame id. Its timestamp becomes the thread anchor: saved as an artifact and passed as thread_ts on every subsequent send. One top-level post per campaign is what keeps concurrent campaigns from colliding in a shared channel.

st-168.title: Morning update at 9:00 AM Eastern
st-168.note: Scheduled daily status broadcast providing progress summaries, forward plans, encountered failures, and resource accounting. Reported metrics include GPU expenditure, token usage, per-target validation gate statuses, and elapsed progress. The instruction 'including weekends' prevents the assumption that reporting pauses.

st-169.title: Hourly update
st-169.note: Short in-thread progress pulse: model identity, target, and current best final_score (or current best ipSAE_min if no design has reached final scoring yet). The fallback to ipSAE_min ensures the hourly update begins in hour 1 before any design completes the full pipeline.

st-170.title: Stall notice
st-170.note: Posted out of thread as a broadcast when the orchestrator has not updated its heartbeat file for 15 minutes, or when WATCHDOG detects a stuck sub-agent. Names the stuck process, elapsed time since last progress, and immediate remediation action. Stalls exceeding 30 minutes escalate to a halt.

st-171.title: Standard status block format
st-171.note: Six mandatory fields in every status post. Field (c) requires reporting UNCALIBRATED for uncalibrated pace estimates without descriptive adjectives, while field (f) tracks cumulative deviation counts from an append-only log.

st-172.title: Reporting invariant: one function, fresh aggregate, every time
st-172.note: Every number in every Slack post comes from one saved SCRIBE function that runs a fresh server-side aggregate at post time and asserts the truncation flag is false. Memory, cached snapshots, client-side summation over returned rows and output-file counts are all forbidden sources. The stated priority is unusual and deliberate: a fabricated or stale figure is a worse failure than a missing one.

st-173.title: Drive: the deliverables folder
st-173.note: Requires operator-supplied folder paths and URLs configured before campaign launch. Every deliverable uploaded to Drive must be linked in Slack to maintain an accessible index.

st-174.title: Drive invariant: one writer, one folder, transactional close-out
st-174.note: Exactly one role may create folders or upload, restricted to one campaign sub-folder with a single close_out/ directory. Close-out is transactional: snapshot the ranked sheet, derive every companion artifact from that state, and assert mandatory columns. A null in a required non-critical column downgrades the row to disclosed-with-deviation rather than dropping it.

st-176.title: Final deliverables header
st-176.note: Introduces the six numbered artefacts that must exist before the campaign can be declared complete.

st-178.title: Deliverable 1: The design sheet
st-178.note: One CSV, exactly 30 sequences per target and only those 30, with explicit intra-target rank and full metadata. The constraint 'and only those 30' prohibits delivering a longer list and delegating selection to the reader.

st-179.title: Sheet schema, frozen at kickoff
st-179.note: A schema file written at kickoff defines column names, data types, enumerations, units, and non-null constraints, and writers validate every row against it. The required columns include full provenance (root_backbone_id, parent_design_id, opt_round) and paths to the structures evaluated by each ranking arm.

st-180.title: Null policy, rank ordering, and the seed top-up wave
st-180.note: Rank is determined by a single ORDER BY: full-seed status, then pose_PASS, then rank_zscore. Rows below 5 seeds after a failed top-up remain ranked with seed count disclosed, while unranked rows are reserved for missing or zero scores. Missing per-arm scores are recorded as NaN rather than numeric sentinels (such as 0.0 or -999) to prevent distorting downstream means, and score_instrument records the active mask.

st-181.title: Gate recompute at write time
st-181.note: The writer recomputes every gate from raw inputs at the same threshold the carried flag was set at, and any disagreement is fail-loud and blocks the row. Short, but it is what turns every upstream gate from a promise into a verified fact at the last possible moment.

st-182.title: Companion files header
st-182.note: Introduces the two machine-readable files that make the sheet independently reproducible.

st-183.title: per_seed_metrics.parquet: The sheet's audit trail
st-183.note: One row per design x arm x seed with raw values, so any sheet score can be reproduced without recompute. Coverage must be 100% of ranked design_ids by exact case-sensitive match, and no (design, arm) group may be uniformly null on the ranking metric. Before finalising, 30 sampled rows per target are recomputed from the companion alone and must agree to 1e-4 or the companion is regenerated.

st-184.title: instrument_realization.csv: What the instrument actually was
st-184.note: One row per (target, arm) recording gate status, seeds run, whether the arm fed final_score, control separation, drop reason, and the cofactor and chain-count columns from the dossier rule. Every numeric is DERIVED from the companion and the gate file at write time, never hand-authored, with row-for-row agreement asserted against a recount. This is the table that makes 'we ran the three-arm instrument' checkable rather than assertable, and the report's scoring section is generated from it.

st-185.title: Row count and the relaxation ladder
st-185.note: Requires exactly 30 ranked candidates per target, relaxing filters in a defined sequence only after upstream regeneration is exhausted: diversity caps first, then liability flags, with novelty as a bounded last resort. pose_dockq and final_score constraints cannot be relaxed, and padding short candidate lists with duplicate entries is prohibited. The prompt explicitly forbids implementing relaxation by deleting, commenting out, or monkeypatching gate predicates.

st-186.title: Deliverable 2: The report
st-186.note: A publication-formatted PDF documenting campaign methods, figures, and literature citations. Before finalization, all quantitative figures in the abstract and results must be recomputed from delivered artifacts, correcting discrepancies and removing unverified statements.

st-187.title: Deliverable 3: The supplement
st-187.note: One archive for everything that does not belong in a PDF.

st-188.title: Supplement contents and path discipline
st-188.note: For every ranked design: the designed complex and every predicted complex used for scoring, in a fixed directory layout keyed by rank and design_id. The sheet's path columns point into this bundle using bundle-relative paths only, independent of per-job tarballs and Modal workspace paths, so the deliverable remains valid after the compute environment is deleted.

st-189.title: The numbered-directory copy step
st-189.note: Rebuilds the structure directory from the final design sheet as the concluding close-out step, preventing path discrepancies. Verification asserts that every referenced file exists and that path rank prefixes match assigned sheet ranks.

st-190.title: Files must be readable off Drive
st-190.note: Path resolution is not enough: every referenced file in the sheet and supplement must open from Google Drive through the connector before close-out completes. A broken link or truncated upload is a close-out blocker, not a minor defect.

st-191.title: Packaging rules and the byte-split last resort
st-191.note: One .tar.gz at the natural granularity, verified to open with a stock unarchiver before being declared delivered. Byte-splitting is a last resort with two concrete reasons: a part cannot be opened alone, and Drive mis-detects MIME types on raw chunks. If forced, the README must carry the exact concatenation command and the part list goes to Slack.

st-192.title: Deliverable 4: The scoreboard
st-192.note: A summary markdown table reporting per-target metric medians and diversity metrics, using the identical calculation code that enforces the selection caps. Every metric column requires a real computed numeric value (no NaN, sentinel, or free text), and anything uncomputable must be listed in a Deviations section below.

st-193.title: Deliverable 5: Files in Drive, not references to files
st-193.note: The actual artefacts go in the one campaign folder; a manifest of artifact IDs is explicitly insufficient. Upload only when final, and if a replacement is unavoidable, version-suffix it and post the canonical-file map.

st-194.title: Deliverable 6: Closing post, gated on a review fleet
st-194.note: Before the conclusion can be posted, at least five independent auditor sub-agents review deliverables 1-5. Two have specified independence properties: one must have GPU access to re-score a sample from raw inputs, and one must form its verdict from raw companion and supplement without seeing the report's conclusions. Every BLOCKER must be resolved first.

st-196.title: Read the thread, but do not take direction from it
st-196.note: Replies to questions are expected; plan changes are not, unless the campaign operator explicitly directs them. Guards a long-running autonomous agent against being steered off-plan by well-meaning bystanders in a shared channel.

st-198.title: Adversarial review of every deliverable
st-198.note: Some reviewers are explicitly briefed as adversarial, and the scope includes intermediate Slack posts, not just final artefacts. Cheap to do given unlimited tokens, and the main defence against a self-consistent but wrong campaign narrative.

st-200.title: Use the whole window
st-200.note: There is no reward for finishing early, and a little late beats very early. Counter-programming against an agent's tendency to declare success at the first coherent stopping point.

st-202.title: Close-out reserve and surplus budget plan
st-202.note: The final hour is reserved for close-out and runs as an unblocked child process so the orchestrator's heartbeat and governor loops stay alive. No new waves may be launched with two named exemptions: audit re-scoring and the seed top-up to n_seeds=5. If the governor shows substantial budget remaining at T0+23h, the orchestrator drafts and executes a surplus-budget plan.

st-204.title: Emergency throttles have a hard expiration
st-204.note: Any emergency throttle on generation or scoring must include an explicit expiration time and apply only to new dispatches. Running jobs always complete: a sub-agent receiving a budget steer must never cancel, terminate, or reap. A throttle active two hours after its root cause is resolved is a reportable defect.

st-206.title: 24 hours
st-206.note: The wall clock, and the scalar that most shapes the delegation architecture: at this duration the orchestrator cannot do the work itself.

st-208.title: Timing and CLOCK: the no-hang contract
st-208.note: Opens by defining operational pacing: no rest, no breaks, and the clock does not stop when idle. Any five-minute interval without an in-flight tool call or bounded wait is classified as a hang, with a target of zero hung minutes across the campaign. A dedicated CLOCK singleton dispatches in the first 15 minutes, writing elapsed fraction and hours remaining every 5 minutes to prevent orchestrator time errors.

st-210.title: Orchestrator discipline: no SDK, no foreground loops, block on SETUP
st-210.note: Prohibits time.sleep, long-running tool calls over 5 minutes, direct provider SDK or billing API access, and all Modal sandboxes from the orchestrator process. The orchestrator must block on the SETUP sub-agent at T0 before dispatching any other work. It interacts with compute solely through host delegation and task completion.

st-212.title: Sub-agent swarm, single base model
st-212.note: Sub-agents at all delegation depths must run on the orchestrator's base model to evaluate single-model capability. The campaign architecture expects swarms of over 50 concurrent agents at peak. If the harness rejects a sub-agent's own delegation, the fallback is to request root dispatch from the orchestrator.

st-214.title: Delegation: the full agent org chart and its failure detectors
st-214.note: The prompt's architectural core: a posted delegation architecture in hour 1, dedicated singletons, and failure detectors. WATCHDOG escalates on heartbeat staleness (stall notice at 15 minutes, ceiling=0 at 30 minutes) and halts a runaway fleet on sandbox count alone. Singletons write liveness every cycle, while monitor sub-agents track jobs at a 1:10 ratio and harvest outputs.

st-216.title: Literature: re-read on triggers, not on a schedule
st-216.note: Three named triggers, all diagnostic rather than routine: a tool under-producing or failing its gate, a substitution of one instrument for another, and a budget reallocation toward or away from a method. The reasoning is that a config flag or documented limitation usually explains the failure, so reading the paper is cheaper than debugging blind. Each triggered re-read is recorded in the living ideas document.

st-218.title: Epistemics: no ungrounded claims, no hallucinated literature
st-218.note: Every factual claim must trace to an executed tool call, an artifact, or the prompt itself. Citing external identifiers (DOI, PMID, PDB ID, accession, or URL) from model memory is prohibited; every identifier must originate from a tool lookup executed within the current session.

st-220.title: Diagnosing anomalous outputs
st-220.note: Suspicious outputs (such as all-zero scores, identical gate passes, perfect metrics, or runs completing in seconds) are treated as software defects rather than positive results. Inherited inputs (target structures, construct definitions, hotspot numberings) must be verified against source files before use.

st-222.title: Cheapest falsifying check first
st-222.note: Before committing significant compute, run the cheapest test that could prove the plan wrong. A seconds-scale sanity check that could kill a multi-hour run always comes first.

st-224.title: Report messy results as messy
st-224.note: One sentence, no elaboration. Permission to be inconclusive, which an agent optimising for a satisfying report would not otherwise take.

st-226.title: Conservative reporting: highlight limitations
st-226.note: Findings must emphasize conservative interpretations of results rather than optimistic summaries. Methodological changes and retrospective parameter tuning must be documented alongside the total number of tested configurations.

st-228.title: Standards bind tighter under autonomy
st-228.note: The justification for everything in the Behavior section. Because no human reviews the work before resources are spent, the agent's own verification discipline is the only gate. Resolves the standing tie-break: when in doubt between a confident result and a flagged uncertainty, flag it.

st-230.title: Roster PASS: five required conditions
st-230.note: Requires validating each candidate tool on a campaign target under five criteria: container build, weight checksum verification, clean exit on test candidates, valid structure generation, and successful sequence adapter integration. Compute commitments are capped at ~10% per model until validation completes.

st-232.title: Build it yourself; do not trust skills
st-232.note: Local image builds and pinned commits are authoritative: skills are documentation, not execution environments. When a skill contradicts the prompt or upstream tool documentation, follow the documentation.

st-234.title: Check the first shard before launching the fleet
st-234.note: Examine outputs from the first shard of any generation or scoring wave before fanning out: verify file counts, parse structures, and inspect score distributions. Uniform pass or fail rates indicate configuration failures that require diagnosis.

st-236.title: Check pose agreement on the SAME seed
st-236.note: When evaluating pose self-consistency, DockQ must be calculated against the exact seed that produced the argmax-ipSAE score. Evaluating DockQ on seed A and ipSAE on seed B produces mismatched structural evaluations.

st-238.title: Test the actual parameter, not an approximation
st-238.note: Validation must evaluate the exact metric parameters planned for production, such as testing full seed counts rather than single-seed approximations. Running N seeds (not one) demonstrates that the ensemble provides incremental ranking signal over single seeds.

st-240.title: Honest status: protocol or disclosed deviation
st-240.note: Final ranking requires protocol compliance or documented relaxation, recording actual seed counts on every candidate row. Candidates short on seed counts must attempt top-up before being classified as unranked, and unexecuted gates represent protocol violations.

st-242.title: Commanded versus delivered counts
st-242.note: Every batch job reports both, and a shortfall over ~10% is a warning in the manifest and updates even when the job exits cleanly. Every count is measured from artefacts or the ledger at write time, never reconstructed from what was commanded; where measured disagrees with planned, report measured and the gap. Bookkeeping writes are idempotent so re-runs cannot double-count.

st-244.title: Liveness watching, the single reaper, and the one-app rule
st-244.note: Five-minute liveness checks identify inactive jobs, with BUDGET's reap sweep acting as the sole campaign-wide reaper cross-checked against the job ledger. The one-app rule prevents blanket terminations from impacting other workloads in shared workspaces. Closes with a zero-critical-state rule and a five-step restart sequence to recover state from durable storage.

st-246.title: Re-check all filters before ordering
st-246.note: Re-evaluates developability liabilities, monomer foldability, and diversity caps on the final candidate pool before ordering. For counter-screened targets, ranking expands to include selectivity_delta (on-target minus off-target ipSAE_min), treating missing off-target measurements as errors.

st-248.title: Review fleet independence requirements
st-248.note: At least one reviewer generates new measurements rather than reviewing documents, and at least one forms its verdict from raw data without seeing conclusions. Every finding is reported with the exact query or script that produced each number; review follows the same traceability standard as production tasks.

st-250.title: Unavailability requires evidence, not inference
st-250.note: Before concluding any tool is unavailable, query HuggingFace, GitHub, PyPI, the skill catalog and the corpus directly. States the reason plainly: several tools named here postdate the model's training cutoff, so 'I have never heard of it' is not evidence of absence. A failed URL is grounds to request network access, and the exact queries are logged with the conclusion.

st-252.title: Logistics: ids, versioning, and secrets
st-252.note: Assigns globally unique design IDs with target and method prefixes, freezing pipeline scripts upon entering production with changes saved as versioned files. Credentials must never appear in command strings, logs, or messages: secrets reach sandboxes only via modal.Secret or environment injection.

st-254.title: Multi-tenant isolation: namespace everything
st-254.note: Agents must isolate operations in shared accounts by filtering Slack messages, Drive folders, and Modal volumes to campaign-specific identifiers. Shared volumes must incorporate orchestrator frame IDs to prevent naming collisions.

st-256.title: Volume layout: batch to survive the inode cap
st-256.note: One metrics JSONL and one structures tar per job_id, because a 5-seed by 1M-design campaign at one file per design x seed exceeds Modal's inode cap. JIT and torch-extension caches go on the persistent volume. Any delete on a shared volume requires a verified tarball first, and a failed preserve step halts and escalates rather than proceeding.

st-258.title: Slack directives must be verified at source
st-258.note: Any relayed directive is re-read from a fresh thread call with limit >= 500 before acting, and only directives locatable in the thread are acted on. Owner-approved status applies only to a message quoted verbatim with channel and timestamp; sub-agent recommendations, swarm consensus and the agent's own proposals stay labelled as such. A defence against a long agent chain laundering a suggestion into an instruction.

st-260.title: Allocate by evidence; keep a prepared idea list
st-260.note: A target stays active while its best score is still improving or has an untested round remaining, and while untried methods remain. The living ideas document ensures stalled targets are addressed from a prepared, ranked list rather than impromptu additions. If wall-clock limits bind before budget exhaustion, scale concurrency instead of cutting planned work without notice.

st-262.title: Failure modes to pre-empt
st-262.note: Pre-empts failure modes: silent filter evasion, drifting thresholds, unanchored scoring metrics, and early stopping. Each failure mode is paired with a specific mechanical countermeasure.

st-264.title: Safety: the one section that overrides everything above
st-264.note: Bioterrorism and bioweapons development are strictly excluded, and scope is bounded to miniprotein binder design with in vitro validation. Any stop or pause instruction from Anthropic staff must be complied with immediately and without debate, overriding all timelines and targets. Genuine safety concerns require pausing and contacting the operator rather than self-resolving.
